**The operator guide no longer implies the sandbox covers this.** `Sandbox:AllowNetwork: false` governs repository code in the container; the retrieval tools reach out from the harness process and do not pass that seam. The guarantee it does make is unchanged and still stated — untrusted repository code cannot phone home — with the addition that in `Replay`, which is what `suite` and `ablate` run, nothing is reached at all.

`mcp-retrieval.html` is a description rather than a proposal, and says plainly what did **not** ship: no fixture whose answer is outside the repository, and no arms, so the feature has been shown to work and not shown to help. `docs/index.html`'s proposal table says the same.

**The settings dialog got a Retrieval tab after all — the argument against it did not survive being looked at.** It was that an arm is a configuration file and a saved preference would ride along with arms that did not override it. True, but `Git` and `Sandbox` have had tabs since tasks 40 and 34, and `Git:Enabled` is exactly the same kind of switch: one that decides whether a set of tools reaches the model's schema. A rule that disqualifies retrieval disqualifies those too. The layering claim was also half backwards — a `--config` arm wins *over* saved settings, so an arm that names retrieval was never at risk.

The residual risk is real and belongs somewhere else: an arm that says *nothing* about a lever inherits whatever is saved. That is true of git today. **The fix is `StandardArms` naming its levers, not the UI hiding one** — `Baseline` now pins Critique, Orchestration, bash, both retrieval servers and `Mode=Replay` explicitly, every other arm is built from it by moving one key, and `Every_standard_arm_changes_exactly_one_lever` measures the difference from baseline rather than counting dictionary entries. `with-learn`, `with-code-search` and `with-retrieval` join the catalogue as a `retrieval` set.

The tab is deliberately minimal: switches, mode, corpus folder and budgets. The per-server tool allow-lists stay in configuration files, because which two of a server's tools to register — and what to tell the model they are for — is arm-shaped rather than preference-shaped.

Fixed on the way, and not only in the new tab: a `CheckBox` whose `Content` is a string parses it for access-key mnemonics, so the Git tab had been rendering *"Advertise gitstatus, gitcommit, gitsync, gitpush and create_pull_request"* since task 40. Four labels moved to a `TextBlock`.

## 64. The tool inventory belongs in About, with what each one is for

- [x] **Estimated time:** 0.5d

**Done first, and deliberately before the retrieval branch.** Tasks 54-63 add tool sets behind switches, and this is the surface that has to be able to say which of them a session actually registered. Building it against the two switches that exist today - git and bash - proves the shape on a case that can be tested now, and leaves task 57 nothing to do but be discovered.

The shell announces the tool list once, in the status bar, and then loses it. `MainWindowViewModel` builds `"Ready. 13 tools: update_todos, list_changes, read_file, …"` as the opening `Status`, which wraps to two lines of a one-line surface and is overwritten by the first thing that happens. Names alone were never the useful part: the question anyone actually has is what this thing can do, and a comma-separated list of identifiers does not answer it. About already holds the registry and already reports the count — it is the right home, and it is a surface someone opens deliberately rather than one that shouts at startup.

**Every tool the build knows about is listed, active or not.** A list of only what is registered answers "what can it do right now" and hides the more useful question, which is what it could do and what is switching it off. Five of eighteen are absent on a default install — the git set, `bash`, and soon the retrieval tools — and each absence is a configuration decision somebody made, not a gap in the product. Showing them greyed with the switch that governs them turns About from a status readout into the capability map, and it is what makes "which arm am I actually running" answerable at a glance once task 57 lands.

- [x] Drop the names from the opening `Status`. `ToolNames` on `MainWindowViewModel` has exactly one consumer and becomes dead with it. `PhaseCheckpoint.ToolNames` in `GlassCoder.Lab` is a different property with its own tests and is not touched.
- [x] **`IToolRegistry.Functions` cannot be the only source, and this is the substance of the task.** A disabled tool set is never registered *and never constructed* — with `Git:Enabled` false, `AddGitTools` is not called, `GitTool` does not exist in the container, and no `AIFunction` is built, so there is no description to read. That is deliberate and must stay: gating registration rather than execution is what keeps a switched-off tool out of the model's schema entirely.
- [x] So discover the full set by **reflecting over types, not instances**: scan the `GlassCoder.Tools` assembly for `IToolSet` implementations and their `[GlassCoderTool]` methods, reading `Name`, `Order` and `[Description]` off the `MethodInfo`. No construction, no dependencies, no DI — and it cannot silently miss a tool, because it keys on the same attribute `ToolFunctionFactory` does.
- [x] **Retrieval tools are the exception and need their own source.** They are adapted from a server at run time, not `[GlassCoderTool]` methods, so reflection will not find them. List them from the per-server `Tools` allow-lists in `RetrievalOptions` — available from configuration without connecting to anything — paired with the locally authored descriptions task 57 requires anyway. That is the natural home for those strings.
- [x] Active is membership in `IToolRegistry.Functions`. For an active tool the description is `AIFunction.Description` — literally what was sent — and for an inactive one it is the `[Description]` attribute, which is the string that *would* be sent. Same text by construction; a test asserts they agree for tools that are on, so the two paths cannot drift.
- [x] **An inactive row names the switch that governs it**, because "inactive" alone invites "how do I turn it on": `Git:Enabled`, `Sandbox:EnableBashTool`, `Retrieval:Learn:Enabled`. This mirrors the operator guide's "defaults that refuse", where each refusal names its setting.
- [x] No second set of human-facing prose anywhere. The descriptions are already a line or two and they are what the model is told; a parallel copy would be a third place to keep correct and the first to go stale. It also makes About a cheap review surface for the prompt — a description that reads badly to a person very likely reads badly to the model, and fixing it improves both.
- [x] `AboutWindow.xaml` is `Height="392"` with `ResizeMode="NoResize"`; eighteen or more rows will not fit beside the existing content. Grow the window and put the list in a `ScrollViewer` below the divider and above the build line, in advertised order, with inactive rows visually distinct rather than hidden or sorted away — a switched-off tool sitting in its own place in the order is part of what the list is saying.
- [x] Optional, and it fits what this application is for: each active tool's schema character count on its row. About then becomes the profile inspector — what exists, what is on, what each is for, and what each costs on every request — which puts the number from task 58 where someone would look for it rather than only in a test's output.
- [x] Tests in `GlassCoder.Wpf.Tests`: every registered function appears and is marked active; a tool set switched off appears and is marked inactive with its switch named; the union is stable whichever switches are on; descriptions agree between the two sources for active tools; and `Status` no longer contains a tool name.

The reflection sweep has a second use worth noting when it is written: a tool type that appears in no registration path at all — enabled or disabled — is a defect this list would show, and that class of dormancy is real here. `ModelContextProtocol` sat pinned and referenced by nothing for the whole life of the project.

**Shipped as `ToolCatalog` in `GlassCoder.Tools`, and one bullet turned out not to be needed.** The catalogue joins the type sweep to the live registry and returns `ToolCatalogEntry` — name, description, order, active, schema size, and the setting that would switch an inactive tool on. `AboutViewModel` renders those into rows, because the phrasing of "off" belongs on the WPF side of the seam and a record in `GlassCoder.Tools` has no business knowing how a window words things. Twenty-two tools on a default install, thirteen active.

## 65. The screen gets an oracle, and it is a person

- [x] **Estimated time:** 0.5d

Every other claim a run makes is judged by something. Compile is judged by Roslyn, tests by their own exit code, the diff by a panel of critics. What was actually *on the screen* is judged by nobody — which is how run `ea9a1f66` shipped a multiply dialog whose result field sat below the bottom of the window, past a green build, green tests and 100% tool-call validity. The refutation loops that cost `216360bf` twenty-eight steps were three critics reaching for evidence no static check can produce and no worker can supply.

So the one person who can answer is asked, at the one moment they can answer honestly: when the application they launched closes.

- [x] `IDesktopShell.LaunchApp` takes an optional exit callback. Detachment was always about ownership rather than ignorance — the harness still neither drives nor closes the app, it only notices that it is over. `dotnet run` outlives the build and ends when the app does, so the callback fires when the window is shut.
- [x] A strip in the workspace pane, not a modal dialog. A box on top of whatever the operator turned to next gets answered to make it go away, and a rating given to dismiss something is worse than no rating. **Skip** is a first-class button for the same reason.
- [x] Score 0–5, comment optional and kept verbatim. Recording is disabled until a score is chosen, so an empty answer cannot be recorded by pressing the obvious button.
- [x] Recorded as a `Role: "human"` step through `IStepLogger`, under the tool name `operator_rating` — the precedent the manual Commit and Push buttons set. A step rather than a new record type because it then lands in the JSONL transcript and the live view with no new reader, and replays with the run it judged. It carries `rating`, `outOf`, `application` and `comment`, and `outOf` is written down so no reader has to assume the scale.
- [x] Attributed to the run whose changes the pane is showing — a verdict on a window is a verdict on the work that built it — and to no run when the operator ran the app without one.
- [x] Tests: the question waits for the close and is never asked after a failed launch, recording is refused without a score, the comment round-trips trimmed, an unwritten comment is null rather than blank, and Skip records nothing.

Acceptance: closing a launched application asks for a rating; recording it puts an `operator_rating` step in the transcript against the right run; skipping leaves no trace. Depends on tasks 11, 39.

**A test caught itself passing for the wrong reason.** The exit callback arrives on a background thread and marshals to the UI one, so the first version read the strip's state before the pane had been told and four tests went green against a question that had never been asked. They pump the dispatcher now, and the helper that does it says why.

`FakeShell` moved out of `TestRunConvenienceTests` into its own file on the way: two tests drive the workspace pane, and two fakes of one seam drift apart exactly where it matters.

**Not done: the rating does not reach `metrics.jsonl`.** Metrics are written when a run ends and the rating arrives afterwards, so recording it there means either rewriting a finished line or a second line per run that every reader has to join. Both are worse than a transcript entry that is already replayable and already grepped. Revisit when an arm actually wants to compare operator scores — which is task 61's problem, and it will want the fixture from task 60 first.

## 66. Notice when a test suite exercises nothing

- [x] **Estimated time:** 1.5d

Run `122e11c6` produced five passing tests that never call the application. Every one of them multiplies two literals with the `*` operator and asserts the answer:

```csharp
double firstNumber = 5.0;
double secondNumber = 3.0;
double result = firstNumber * secondNumber;   // the test computes it itself
Assert.Equal(15.0, result);
```

`using MultiplyApp;` is present and unused. The `ProjectReference` exists and is never exercised. Delete the entire application and all five still pass — they assert that .NET can multiply doubles.

**That suite satisfied every oracle this harness has.** Compile green, `run_tests` green, the ladder's UnitTests rung passed, the completion critique accepted 1/3 on the strength of "build and tests pass", the post-run review accepted 3/3, and the operator rated the running window 5/5. Nothing was wrong with any of those judgements: the window really was right, and the tests really did pass. **Nothing in the harness asks whether the tests touch the product**, and that is a missing oracle in the harness-advisor's own sense — a run that clears every rung and still fails the thing the rungs stand for.

It is also not a model failure to route around. The logic lives inside `MultiplyButton_Click`, so there was no seam a test could reach; the model wrote the only tests the design allowed. A notice that fires here is therefore evidence about the *design*, which is the more useful thing to say.

- [x] **Syntax tree only.** For each test source, collect the identifiers its method bodies actually use, and ask whether any is declared by a workspace source outside the test project - the sweep `FindSymbolTool.Declares` already runs, through the analyzer's cache. No reference resolution, so none of the false-negative risk that kept `find_references` unbuilt (task 48).
- [x] **A notice, never a gate.** The signal is good, not certain: tests that drive the product through DI, reflection or a launched process would look identical to tests that drive nothing. This repository has twice been taught what a confident refusal costs - the gate deadlocks of `5c071f37` and `a408b61b`, and the XAML handler pre-check that was designed and then dropped for exactly this reason. It rides the `run_tests` summary and the ladder's rung report; it refuses nothing.
- [x] **It has to reach the critics.** The moment that matters is when a green suite is about to be read as proof, and the panel reads the verification summary. A notice the critics cannot see would leave "build and tests pass" meaning what it means today.
- [x] Word it as the question rather than the verdict: *"these tests reference no type from the projects they depend on - they may not be exercising the code under test"*. Naming the referenced-but-unused assembly is what makes it actionable.
- [x] **Second clause, added from run `d5edbc59` (2026-08-08): a product type only the tests use.** That run's tests *do* call a workspace type - `MultiplyViewModel` - so the first clause stays silent on them, and they are exactly as hollow: the application multiplies inline in `MultiplyButton_Click`, and nothing outside the test file references the class. Ask the same sweep one question further - is a workspace type outside the test projects referenced *only* by test sources? - and word it the same way: *"the tests exercise `<Type>`, which no non-test source references"*. A type reached through DI, reflection or a launched process is a known false positive, which is the third reason this is a notice and not a gate.
- [x] **Third clause: an assertion that cannot fail.** Two of the same run's seven tests compute the expected value with the expression under test - `double expected = 1.234 * 5.678` against a `Multiply` that *is* `a * b` - so they hold for any implementation of that shape and their precision arguments are decorative. Both were edited into that form to clear a real failure. Syntax alone catches it: inside a test method, an assertion whose expected argument is a non-literal expression whose identifier set is a subset of the identifiers passed to the call under test. *"expected is computed from the same operands passed to the method under test; this assertion cannot fail."*
- [x] Tests: a suite that calls a workspace type is silent; one that only asserts over literals is noticed; one that reaches its subject through a variable or a helper is silent; a project with no `ProjectReference` at all is silent, because there is nothing it was supposed to exercise. For the second clause, `MultiplyViewModel` as that run left it is noticed and the same tree with the click handler calling it is silent. For the third, `MultiplyViewModelTests.cs:80` and `:95` are noticed and `:20`, `:35`, `:50`, `:65`, `:110` - all carrying independently-known literals - are not.

Acceptance: the `CalculatorTests.cs` this task was written from produces a notice, a suite that calls `Calculator.TryMultiply` does not, and run `d5edbc59`'s tree produces a notice naming `MultiplyViewModel` and one naming its two tautological assertions. Depends on tasks 17, 47.

**Built as `TestSuiteNotices`, on the `XamlNotices` pattern**: a static sweep returning notice text that a caller appends to its own summary verbatim. It rides two places rather than one - the `run_tests` summary *and* `TestRunResult.Notices`, which the ladder's UnitTests rung renders. The rung matters more than the tool: the ladder builds its own sentence and would otherwise have dropped the notice, and the rung report is what the critics read when they decide whether "tests pass" means the work is done.

**The false positive that had to be bought off is XAML.** A view model reached only through a `DataContext` is driven by the application at runtime, and calling it untested would be plainly wrong - so markup is swept for the type name and counts as a reference. DI and reflection remain known false positives, which is the third reason this is a notice rather than a gate.

**The tautology rule is deliberately narrow.** Expected must be a *computed* expression, not a literal - a wrong literal is a bug the test can catch, which is the point of one - and every identifier in it must be among the arguments handed to the call under test. It follows a local one hop to its initializer, because both of run `d5edbc59`'s assertions were written that way, and no further: a value laundered through three variables is not the observed pattern and chasing it would trade precision for reach.

**Writing the tests found the fixture bug rather than a code bug.** Two of them isolated the tautology clause over a product whose `Calculator` nothing shipping referenced - so the orphan clause fired, correctly, and the assertion of silence failed. The fixture grew an `App` that calls `Calculator`. A notice that fires on a half-built fixture is the notice working.

874 tests green, +7.

**The scope widened before the task was built, and the reason is worth keeping.** This was written from run `122e11c6`, whose tests called nothing at all. Run `d5edbc59` produced the same defect one indirection deeper - a real class, really called, referenced by nothing that ships - and the notice as originally specified would have stayed silent on the very next occurrence of what it was written for. Three consecutive desktop runs have now shipped a suite that verifies nothing about the product, in three different shapes. The clauses are three questions on one sweep, not three tasks.

**Why this is worth more than it looks.** Task 60 is stuck on finding a fixture whose answer the worker does not already know. This is the opposite and cheaper problem: a defect the worker produces *reliably*, on a goal it otherwise solves cleanly, which every existing oracle waves through. Three consecutive runs of the desktop goal have now shipped it. If the notice changes what the next run writes, that is a measurable harness improvement on a task suite that already exists - no new fixture required.

**Not in scope: judging test quality.** Coverage, assertion strength and whether a test is meaningful are all somebody else's problem. This asks one question - does the suite mention the product at all - and stops there.

## 67. The run gets a retrospective, and the harness reads its own report

- [x] **Estimated time:** 5.5d

A fourth surface beside Transcript, Changes and Metrics: **Retrospective**. After a completed run, one button has headless Claude Code produce three things - a code review of what the run built, a review of the run process that built it, informed by that code review, and a checklist of recommended improvements to GlassCoder and its tools. Ticked recommendations become a Markdown work order a fresh code agent implements in this repository. It automates the ritual the `GrokReview*.md` files record by hand; the reviewed task description and the why behind each decision below is `TASK-RetrospectiveSurface.md`.

The mechanism is task 43's, generalised from one file to a run. The three outputs are three subjects in three places - the produced code in the workspace, the process in the transcript under `%LocalAppData%`, the harness in this repository - so no single session can honestly do all three. One orchestrator runs three staged headless sessions: stage 2 receives stage 1's report, stage 3 receives both, each stage with its own directive, budget and timeout, and a failed stage keeps the finished ones' reports.

- [x] First extract the reusable halves of `ClaudeCodeFileReviewer` - launch assembly, envelope parsing, the cached probe, scrubbing - into a shared `ClaudeCliSession`, with `FileReviewer` its first caller and its tests green unchanged. Containment stays a constructor fact rather than a caller option: read-only tools, non-writing permission mode, prompt on stdin, key via the environment.
- [x] `RetrospectiveOptions` under `GlassCoder:Retrospective`: per-stage `MaxBudgetUsd` (2.00) and `TimeoutSeconds` (900), `MaxRecommendations` (12), `OutputDirectory` (`.glasscoder/retrospectives`), and `HarnessRepoPath` - the running app knows its build directory and not its source tree, so where work orders land is configured, and the Write button greys with the setting named until it is set.
- [x] **Stage 1 reviews the run's footprint, not the workspace.** The changed files from `IChangeLog`, diff text capped like `RunReviewOptions.MaxChangeCharacters`; a standard code-quality directive with task 66's question inside it - do the tests touch the product - and citations as `path:line`.
- [x] **Stage 2 judges the process, and may quote stage 1.** Its input is the run's step/tool/outcome sequence, extracted and capped into the retrospective's own folder rather than handing the CLI `%LocalAppData%` or raw JSONL - task 15's lesson one level up. It is asked for wasted steps, thrash, refusal loops and oracle gaps, tied to stage 1's defects where the evidence supports it.
- [x] **Stage 3 recommends against this repository.** `--add-dir` on `HarnessRepoPath`; told to read `WORKPLAN.md` and `HISTORY.md` first so it does not re-propose what is done or already planned; at most `MaxRecommendations`, priority-ordered, in task 43's action shape. Only this stage is tickable - stage 1 findings already have their consumption path in the review strip's retry, and a second work-order path for them would blur who acts on what.
- [x] **The minutes are narrated.** `--output-format stream-json --verbose` emits every tool call and assistant message as a line while the CLI works, and `ProcessRunner` already reads stdout line by line - an optional `OnOutputLine` on `ProcessRunRequest` is the entire seam change, set by no existing caller. The surface shows the feed under the stage progress; events marshal to the dispatcher (task 65's exit-callback lesson), lines are scrubbed, an unparseable line is skipped, and a CLI too old to stream falls back to task 43's buffered launch and says so once. Narration never fails a retrospective.
- [x] Each stage persists on completion under `.glasscoder/retrospectives/<runId>/` with `review-actions`-style front matter, so the surface rehydrates after a restart and a crashed stage 3 does not cost stages 1-2. Each stage is recorded as a `Role: "human"` transcript step against the run it judges - the task 43/65 precedent.
- [x] **The finished checklist arrives as a window.** Stage 3 completing opens a non-modal `RetrospectiveResultWindow` - the operator turned to something else minutes ago, and the window arriving is the "it is done". It shares the surface's view model so ticks are the same ticks in both places, closes without loss, reopens from a button on the surface, and never pops on rehydration at startup.
- [x] The work order generalises `ReviewActionFile` (`kind: retrospective-actions`, `target: harness`) and is self-sufficient for a cold agent: run id, goal, the three report paths, every recommendation with the ticked ones marked, and a closing instruction block. It lands in `<HarnessRepoPath>/docs/retrospectives/`, and the write is a transcript step like the git buttons'.
- [x] Tests: the extraction keeps `FileReviewer`'s suite green; the orchestrator over a faked runner launches three times with the right working directories, roots and stdin, stage 2's stdin containing stage 1's report, a failed stage persisting the finished ones, cancellation between stages keeping them, and costs summing; scripted stream lines produce the expected activity events and the final envelope, with garbage skipped; feed tests pump the dispatcher; the window opens once per completed retrospective and never on rehydration; the work order round-trips through the parser, refuses no-ticks and no-`HarnessRepoPath`, and is path-confined like `ReviewActionWriter`.

Acceptance: after a completed run, the Retrospective surface produces three readable reports for that run's id while narrating the work live; the finished checklist opens in a window whose ticked items generate one Markdown work order in this repository that a fresh Claude Code session can implement with no other context; and a missing CLI, a mid-run press and a failed stage each explain themselves. Depends on tasks 11, 12, 43.

**The extraction was the cheap part, and it proved itself immediately.** `ClaudeCliSession` took the launch assembly, the envelope parsing, the cached probe and the scrubbing out of `ClaudeCodeFileReviewer`, whose constructor and eleven tests are untouched - which is what "no behaviour change" is supposed to mean and rarely does. The retrospective then needed none of that written twice, and the streaming variant landed inside the seam rather than beside it, so the file review inherits narration the day something wants it.

**`OnOutputLine` is the whole streaming change on the harness side**, and `ProcessRunner` already read stdout line by line - the callback sits in front of the existing `StringBuilder` append, so a watching caller loses nothing from the buffered result. `FakeProcessRunner` replays scripted stdout through it, because a fake that skipped that would let a streaming caller pass its tests and find nothing to read against the real thing.

**Two decisions came out of writing the fallback rather than planning it.** A CLI too old for `stream-json` refuses the flag before starting a session, so the retry is free - but a session that failed *after* streaming has already done minutes of billable work, and re-running it would silently charge twice. The retry is therefore conditioned on `!Streamed`, not on failure. And `--verbose` turned out to be mandatory with `stream-json` in print mode, which is a technicality nobody would guess from the symptom, so a test asserts the two travel together.

**The results window opens from the view model, through `IRetrospectiveResultDialog`.** The alternative - the shell watching for a finished retrospective - would have put the shell in the business of knowing when a surface's third stage completed. The dialog is single-instance and non-modal, and it shares the surface's view model, so the ticks are one set of ticks and closing it loses nothing.

**One thing is deliberately not automatic: `HarnessRepoPath`.** Until it is set, the work-order button is greyed and names the setting. That is the honest state - the application knows where it was built from, not where its source is - but it does mean the feature is two-thirds useful out of the box, and the third that writes the work order needs one line of configuration first. `%APPDATA%\GlassCoder\settings.json` shadows `config/appsettings.json`, so that is the file to put it in.

819 tests green, +36: thirteen on the orchestrator and its staging, seven on the stream reader and its fallbacks, seven on the work order and its containment, and nine on the surface - including one that lays out both the control and the window over a real retrospective, because the item templates are only instantiated when something asks the panel for its size.

## 68. A capped session keeps the answer it already gave

- [x] **Estimated time:** 0.5d

The first whole retrospective ran on 2026-08-08 against run `d5edbc59`. It produced three reports; the operator saw two. Stage 3 worked for 305 seconds, called `StructuredOutput` successfully at 20:30:37.643 - a full report and nine priority-ordered recommendations - and `ClaudeCliSession` discarded all of it six-tenths of a second later because the process exited 1. The exit was `--max-budget-usd 2` against a session that had spent about $5. The cap is not enforced mid-flight: the session passed $2 in its first minute and worked on for another four, so the money was gone either way and only the answer was lost.

What the log said about it, in full, was `The CLI failed with exit 1: `.

Two defects, both in `ClaudeCliSession.RunOnceAsync`, and the second is why the first took a session log and a token count to find.

- [x] **A session that answered and then exceeded its budget keeps the answer.** `result.ExitCode != 0` returned `Failed` before anything read the envelope. `SalvageableAnswer` now looks first, and a kept answer carries a new `ClaudeCliResult.Caveat` rather than a `Failure`. A session that failed *before* answering is unchanged.
- [x] **The failure says what the CLI said.** Detail fell back to `envelope.Result`, which a budget-exhausted envelope does not carry, so the reason arrived empty. `FailureDetail` now reads stderr, then `errors[]`, then an error-shaped `subtype` with its `terminal_reason`, and only then `result`.
- [x] Raise the defaults now that there is a measurement: `RetrospectiveOptions.MaxBudgetUsd` 2.00 → 8.00, with the three measured stage costs written into the doc comment so the next person changing it argues with a number.
- [x] **Found while testing it: a failed session was recorded as having cost nothing.** The failure path built its result from the reason alone, so a stage cut off after four minutes of paid work reached the transcript at $0.00 with no session id - which is most of why the original incident was hard to trace to a budget at all. Cost and session id now travel with a failure as well as an answer.
- [x] Tests: ten, nine in `ClaudeCliCeilingTests` and one in `RetrospectiveTests` - the capped-with-structured-output shape, the capped prose shape, the streamed route, the capped-with-nothing shape, the subtype-only shape, the unauthenticated guard, stderr still winning, spend recorded on failure, the ceiling default, and a stage-3 cap that persists `3-harness.md` and `recommendations.json`.

Acceptance: replaying stage 3's 2026-08-08 session produces a persisted `3-harness.md` and `recommendations.json` rather than a `not_reviewed` step, and a reader can tell a capped session from a crashed one without leaving the transcript. Depends on task 67.

**The report was recovered by hand, which is the argument for the task.** Claude Code keeps every session at `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/<sessionId>.jsonl`, and the answer is the record whose `attachment.type` is `structured_output`. It was lifted out on 2026-08-09 and written into `.glasscoder/retrospectives/d5edbc59.../` in the shape `Load` rehydrates from, so the surface now shows all three stages and its nine recommendations are tickable. That recovery is also the proof: the data was never lost, only the exit code was consulted.

**The salvage is deliberately asymmetric, and the asymmetry is the whole safety of it.** `structured_output` only exists when the model answered in the requested shape, so it is an answer whatever ended the session. `result` is not: an unauthenticated session writes `"Not logged in · Please run /login"` there and sets `is_error`, and the obvious reading of the task - "keep it if there is a result" - would have filed a broken login as a review. `result` is therefore trusted only when `StoppedAtItsCeiling` holds, which is a statement about spend rather than about the work, and `A_session_that_never_authenticated_is_still_a_failure` is the test that keeps it that way.

**The caveat rides `Failure` on a stage that is `Reviewed`, and no XAML changed.** Both surfaces already render that field beside the report rather than instead of it - `HasFailure` on the retrospective, `ReviewStatus` on the file viewer - so a truncated answer arrives visibly truncated. `ReadRecommendations` concatenates rather than overwrites, because a stage capped before it proposed anything was silent *because* it was capped, and that is the more useful half of the sentence.

**The streamed route is the one that mattered, and it is the one the buffered tests would have missed.** A watched retrospective assembles its envelope from the final `result` event rather than from one buffered blob, so the salvage had to work down that path too - and it had to not wake the `!Streamed` retry, which exists to stop a stage being paid for twice. `The_streamed_route_salvages_it_too_and_never_pays_twice` asserts both halves. Every other test here uses the buffered call, and every one of them would have passed while the real feature stayed broken.

## 69. The rung says which assertion failed, and by how much

- [x] **Estimated time:** 1d

Run `d5edbc59` wrote seven tests at step 15; two failed. Step 16 loosened the tolerance from six decimals to five, which could not possibly help - the literal was wrong by 5×10⁻³, not by rounding. Step 17 replaced the independent expected value with the expression under test, and the suite went green. The correction removed the oracle rather than fixing it, which is the worst repair available to a harness that was holding the right answer.

What the model saw at step 16 was `2 of 7 tests failed: <names>`. What the test runner had said was `Assert.Equal() Failure: Expected: 7.011652, Actual: 7.006652` - and the actual product is exactly what a wrong literal needs to be corrected against.

**The output is not thrown away; it is dropped one level down.** `TestRunResult` carries an `Output` tail (`RunTestsTool.cs:31`, populated at `:148`), so an explicit `run_tests` call does return it. Steps 15-17 never made one - they were `create_file` and `edit_file`, whose verification runs through the ladder, and the ladder builds its rung summary from `FailedTests` names alone and discards `tests.Output` entirely (`VerificationLadder.cs:347`). Two organs, two views of one fact, and the model was reading the narrowed one.

- [x] **The rung summary carries the first failure's message**, on the contract task 15 established: one message per test, three spelled out, and the count stays the true one. `TestOutputParser` gained a `TestFailure` record and reads the block between a test's name and its stack trace; `TestOutputParser.Describe` renders it for both callers.
- [x] The same detail rides the `run_tests` summary line, so the two organs say the same thing whichever one the model asked.
- [x] **The messages go on lines after the count, never inside it.** The run progress sentry keys repeated failures on the first line, so splicing a message into it would make one recurring failure look like a new one every step - the exact confusion that naming the tests was added to remove.
- [x] Tests: five in `SandboxAndParserTests` and one in `VerificationLadderTests` - both numbers reach the observation, each failure keeps its own message without bleeding into the next, a runner that says nothing still parses, `Describe` is empty for no failures and never touches the first line, and the ladder rung carries the assertion while its count line stays byte-identical.

Acceptance: a re-run of the desktop goal that hits a wrong literal corrects the literal instead of replacing it with the expression under test. Depends on tasks 15, 17, 18.

**This is task 45's lesson one rung up.** That task ended a 23-step `edit_file` deadlock by naming *where* the text diverged rather than only that it did. The sibling: **a delta the model cannot see is a repair it cannot make correctly.** Given only "two tests failed", the visible search space holds exactly two moves - loosen the assertion, or set expected to something that must hold - and the run took both, in that order.

**The parser is deliberately tolerant rather than format-specific.** VSTest writes `Error Message:` and `Stack Trace:`; other runners write neither, and a parser that insisted on them would answer nothing at all on the day the format moved - which is the failure this task exists to remove. Whatever sits between a test's name and the next boundary is a better answer than silence. One trap found by testing: the failing-test regex stops on the `[` of `[12 ms]`, so reading from the cursor keeps `12 ms]` as the message; the block starts at the next line.

**The payload gained a field and the prompt budget did not move.** `TestRunResult.Failures` is a return type, and return schemas are not advertised in the tool list - only parameters are. The budget test measures `request.tools`, so this cost nothing on the wire per step. Worth writing down, because the instinct that "a new field costs schema" is right for arguments and wrong here.

856 tests green, +6.

## 70. The zero-match refusal names the way out

- [x] **Estimated time:** 0.5d

`HISTORY.md`'s entry for run `122e11c6` logs this as open and decides against acting on it: steps 9-12 spent on an `edit_file` that would not match, two refusals reading *"None of its lines appear in the file"*, an escape via whole-file `create_file`, *"two wasted steps, self-recovered, one occurrence. Watch rather than fix."*

Run `d5edbc59` is occurrence two. Same steps 9-12, same message, same escape - and this time it cost more than steps: the whole-file rewrite reproduced the WPF template header, which is where the nine unused `using System.Windows.*` directives in that run's code review came from. A targeted edit would not have touched them. By this repository's own decision rule, that makes it a fix.

The message is task 45's improved one and it is factually correct. The cause is not line endings - task 45 matches those flexibly in both directions - but the model quoting text it intended to write. Correct is not the same as actionable: the only move the message offers is re-reading a file the model had already read correctly, which is what step 10 did.

- [x] **Distinguish zero matches from a partial match.** `Nearest` became `Diagnose`, returning the diagnosis *and* the hint that fits it, because the right advice differs by case. The zero-match hint deliberately does not say "read the file again" - re-reading is what the model does anyway and cannot help when the target is text it meant to write.
- [x] **A third case, found while writing the second.** Every line present but the block absent - the quote spans a gap - now says so and asks for one contiguous region. It previously reached `lines[matched]` with `matched == lines.Length` and **threw `IndexOutOfRangeException`**, which any target ending in a newline whose lines all appear somewhere would hit.
- [x] A single-line target that is absent is a zero match too. It used to fall through with no diagnosis at all and inherit the whitespace hint - the one explanation it cannot have.
- [x] Cheap adjacent win in the same seam: `FileReadMemo` records what each file looked like when this run last read it, and `read_file` appends one clause when nothing has changed since.
- [x] Tests: five in `LineEndingTests` - the zero-match refusal names both escape routes and does *not* say to re-read, the single-line case gets the same answer, the scattered case says "not consecutively" instead of throwing, the partial-match refusal keeps its whitespace advice, and an unchanged re-read says so while a write between reads silently makes the next read new again.

Acceptance: the next desktop-goal run that hits this reaches `create_file` in one step rather than four. Depends on tasks 16, 45.

**The memo compares content, not time, and that is what keeps it out of the write tools.** An invalidation call every write path had to remember to make would be one more thing to leave out of the next write path; a digest changes by itself when the file does. It also stores the digest rather than the text, because a run reading twenty files would otherwise hold twenty file bodies for its whole length to answer one yes-or-no question. Keyed by run, on the `VerificationRefusalTracker` pattern, and optional on the constructor so no existing test had to learn about it.

860 tests green, +4.

## 71. The loop can launch what it built

- [x] **Estimated time:** 2d

Twice now a completion critique has refused for want of runtime evidence, and twice the model has had no way to produce any. Run `008007e1` is in `HISTORY.md` for 2026-08-07; run `d5edbc59` is step 22, refuted 3/3, every critic asking for proof that the window shows its result. What was addressed on 2026-08-08 was the gate's wording and its concession behaviour, not the missing capability - so the refutation is still correct and still unanswerable from inside the loop. The only available response is churn, and churn is what the run produced: two XAML attributes, then a re-vote that accepted.

Task 65 built the machinery - `IDesktopShell.LaunchApp`, an exit callback, an `operator_rating` step on close - and gave it to the operator. The loop still has no way to launch anything.

- [x] **`launch_app(projectPath, timeoutSeconds)` - through `IProcessRunner`, not `IDesktopShell`.** The plan named the wrong seam: `IDesktopShell` lives in `GlassCoder.Wpf`, and a tool in `GlassCoder.Tools` cannot reference the UI layer without inverting the dependency direction task 1 set. `dotnet run --project X --no-build` over the process seam is the same capability from the layer that is allowed to have it.
- [x] **Still running at the timeout is the success case, and that inversion is the design.** A WPF application never exits on its own, so "started, drew its window, did not fall over" *is* surviving the clock. Reading it the usual way round would report every working desktop app as a failure and every instant crash as a pass.
- [x] **The result reaches the critics.** `RuntimeEvidence`, keyed by run on the `VerificationRefusalTracker` pattern, holds what the last launch showed; `AgentLoop` appends it to the evidence the completion panel reads. Without that last step a launch would answer the refutation everywhere except where the refutation is made.
- [x] **It runs on the host, and that is a real decision.** The sandbox has no display, so a desktop application cannot start in it - the same reason `GitTool` and the headless reviewers run on the host. What bounds it is the timeout, clamped to 120s however it is asked for, so a hung application costs one step rather than a run.
- [x] **Deliberately not a screenshot.** Pixels are a separate and much larger question. "The application started, stayed up, and did not crash" is already a strictly better evidence base than compile-and-unit-tests, and it is the part available now.
- [x] Tests: seven - still-running counts as started and claims no more than it saw, a crash reports its stderr with `outcomeOk` false, a console app exiting 0 is started, a directory is refused pointing at `list_projects`, the timeout is clamped, and both outcomes reach `RuntimeEvidence`.

Acceptance: the desktop goal's transcript contains a runtime observation, and the "no runtime evidence" refutation either disappears or returns naming what is still missing - the screen - rather than the whole category. Depends on task 65.

**It cost 626 characters of prompt budget on every request, and it was part-paid rather than absorbed.** 168 characters came off first - `run_tests` was describing its own return value, `create_file` carried a phrase written for a human reader, and `launch_app`'s own text was cut by 61 - and the four profile ceilings moved by what was left. The argument is written into `PromptBudgetTests`: this is the only answer the harness has ever had to a refutation it has now received twice, and a tool that turns an unanswerable refusal into an answerable one is worth 157 tokens a step. It is advertised by default, because a tool switched off would leave the refutation exactly as unanswerable.

## 72. The re-vote panel is told whether the evidence moved

- [x] **Estimated time:** 1.5d

`HISTORY.md` records two deadlocks from gates that would not concede - `5c071f37` and `a408b61b` - and the fixes that taught them to. Run `d5edbc59` is the same asymmetry from the other side. At step 22, three critics of three refused for want of runtime evidence. Between then and step 27 the evidence set did not change: same rungs, same summaries, no new step kinds, no runtime anything. Two XAML attributes changed. Two of the three critics flipped to accept.

The panel re-runs up to `MaxCritiquePanels` times (`AgentLoop.cs:234`, assembled at `:652-720`) and each panel reads the current diff fresh. Nothing carries forward what was refused, or whether what would answer it has moved. A gate that cannot tell motion from evidence is not a stricter or a looser gate - it is a gate reading a different question each time it is asked.

- [x] **Carry the prior refutation and a hash of the evidence set into the next panel's prompt.** A run-scoped `CritiqueHistory` holds both; when the fingerprint is unchanged the panel is told what the last one refused and asked to say what changed its mind, "because nothing in the evidence did".
- [x] **The fingerprint is over the evidence, not the diff.** The diff always moves between panels - run `d5edbc59` changed two XAML attributes - and a diff-based hash would have called that new evidence and said nothing. The question is not "did the code move" but "did anything the refutation asked for arrive".
- [x] **Information, never a veto.** This repository has twice paid for an unyielding gate, and the XAML handler pre-check was designed and dropped for the same reason. The critics are told; they still vote, and the run completes exactly as it would have.
- [x] **Persisted as `StepCritiqueRecord.EvidenceUnchanged`** and logged, so "accepted on unchanged evidence" is greppable across runs rather than reconstructed from two transcripts by hand.
- [x] Tests: two - the second panel is handed the first's refusal and told the evidence has not moved while the first panel is told no such thing and the run still completes accepted with the flag set; and a panel that sees a genuinely different rung set is told nothing of the kind.

Acceptance: replaying run `d5edbc59`'s steps 22 to 27 puts the notice in the step-27 panel. Depends on tasks 23, 37.

**Writing the second test made the semantics precise, by failing.** It first tried to produce "new evidence" with a second applied change - and the notice fired anyway, correctly, because the scripted ladder returned the identical rung summaries both times. That is exactly run `d5edbc59`'s shape: an edit is not evidence. The test now enqueues a genuinely different report, and the distinction it defends is the one the task exists for.

- [x] **Estimated time:** 0.5d

Step 1 of run `d5edbc59` created `src/MultiplyApp/solution.slnx` and warned, in the same response, that it is not at the workspace root and builds will not resolve it as their target - *"If you do not need a solution, skip it."* The agent never called `add_to_solution` and never revisited, and an empty `<Solution></Solution>` shipped. The warning was read past, which is what warnings are for.

The artifact is worse than clutter. `dotnet test` against an empty solution runs zero tests and exits 0 - a green that verified nothing, which is the exact failure `RungResult.Unverified` was added to prevent, arriving through a different door.

- [x] **Refuse, with the root path named** - the precedent `HISTORY.md` set on 2026-08-07 for `dotnet_project new`: *"refuse the hazardous scaffold while refusing is one cheap step."* `RefuseSolutionBelowTheRoot` sits beside `RefuseHazardousScaffold` and runs before anything executes.
- [x] **The reason names the consequence, not the rule.** "Builds will not resolve it as their target" was the old warning and was read past; the refusal says that an empty solution makes `dotnet test` run zero tests and exit 0 - a green that verified nothing, which is what `RungResult.Unverified` exists to prevent, arriving through another door.
- [x] **The advice depends on whether the root is writable.** The default writable set is `src` and `tests`, so "create it at the root instead" would often be advice the path guard refuses - one wasted step traded for another. When the root is out of reach the hint says to skip the solution and names what `build` and `run_tests` take instead.
- [x] The now-unreachable warning is gone from `DescribeCreatedSolution` rather than left as dead prose.
- [x] Tests: three - a below-root solution is refused and *nothing runs*, the refusal does not suggest an unwritable root, and a root solution is still created without complaint. Six existing tests that scaffolded solutions under `src` moved to a root-writable guard through a new `RootTool` helper.

Acceptance: the desktop goal produces either no solution or one at the build root, and never an empty one below it. Depends on task 44.

The alternative - allowing below-root solutions for tests only - would have been a rule the tests do not share with production, which is worse than editing six call sites.

- [x] **Estimated time:** 0.5d

Steps 19 and 20 of run `d5edbc59` re-established a green that step 17's inline verification had already reported; steps 25 and 26 re-established step 24's. Four of 28 steps re-confirming the one axis that was never in doubt, in a run where the axis that *was* refuted - runtime behaviour - received none.

`BuildCache` (task 44) already remembers a successful build until the change log moves, and never caches a failure. The same key and the same invalidation apply to a test run with the same target and filter.

## 76. MCP tool registration comes off the UI thread

- [x] **Estimated time:** 2d

Registering MCP tools connects to each configured server to fetch its tool list, and does it on the UI thread. The 2026-08-08 review bounded the wait at 10 seconds, which converts an unbounded hang into a bounded one and is not a fix. A server that is slow, unreachable or behind a captive portal still freezes the window for as long as the bound allows, at startup, which is when a first-run operator is most likely to be watching.

Making registration asynchronous is a real redesign - the registry is built during composition, and tools must exist before the first step can be planned - so it was deliberately kept out of the review fixes rather than smuggled in under one.

- [x] **Decided: start without it and register late.** Registration reads the corpus and never connects. A background refresh asks the server with nobody waiting and writes the list, so the next run has it. The other two options were worse: blocking the first step keeps the freeze and only moves it, and refusing the arm outright throws away a working recorded list because one connection was slow.
- [x] **The old comment's trap is avoided rather than re-entered.** Preferring the recording *forever* was the trap - a renamed tool would never be learned - which is why the blocking call was there. Preferring it *while refreshing* is not the same thing: the refresh is what breaks the loop, and it now writes the corpus in Live as well as Record.
- [x] One refresh in flight per server, so a long-lived process cannot stack connections against a server that is already not answering. Failures are logged and nothing else: this must not make a caller wait, and equally must not make one fail.
- [x] The About inventory reads the state honestly and says "yet" - the list is coming, and the Retrieval tab's record button is the way to have it now. Replay keeps its own wording, because Replay genuinely never connects.
- [x] **`IRetrievalToolLister` extracted so the property is testable at all.** The catalogue depended on the concrete MCP client, and "never waits" cannot be asserted against a real socket. It is a two-method interface that `McpRetrievalUpstream` already satisfied.
- [x] Tests: two - a server that never answers still returns the recorded list in under two seconds, and one that has never been recorded returns nothing just as fast rather than stalling.

Acceptance: with a configured, unreachable MCP server, the application reaches an interactive window in the time it takes without one. Depends on task 57.

885 tests green, +2.
